extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners/petitioners as secondary audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing Section 101 patent-eligibility (judicial exception) analyses, focused on identifying when claim elements do more than merely recite or apply an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon. Advises examiners on considerations, illustrative case law, and how to explain rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere Instructions To Apply An Exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional elements must do more than simply state the judicial exception while adding the words 'apply it' (or an equivalent); mere instructions to implement an abstract idea or other exception on a generic computer do not render the claim patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court authority: Alice (2014) and Mayo (2012) — claims that amount to nothing more than instructing application of the exception using a generic computer are ineligible. Examiners may explain on the record why additional elements do not meaningfully limit the judicial exception. Cross-reference MPEP § 2106.07(a) for formulating eligibility rejections. Courts have found both broad claims eligible and narrow claims ineligible; evaluate each claim on its merits and consult other considerations (improvement, particular machine/transformation, well-understood routine conventionality) to assist the determination. Beware of letting the analysis turn on the draftsman's art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine if the claim merely claims the idea of a solution or outcome without reciting how the solution is accomplished (i.e., result-oriented or functional claiming that covers any solution to an identified problem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Result-oriented claims that attempt to cover any solution with no mechanism or steps for accomplishing the result are equivalent to 'apply it' and do not integrate the exception into a practical application. Case examples: Electric Power Group v. Alstom (claim too result-focused); Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One (claims directed to collecting/displaying/manipulating data without steps of how modifications are performed were ineligible). In contrast, claiming a particular solution or specific way to achieve the outcome may integrate the exception into a practical application. Use these comparisons when explaining a rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the claim invokes computers or other machinery merely as a tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether computers/machinery are used only in their ordinary capacity (tools to perform an existing process) rather than improving computer/technical capabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a computer to receive, store, or transmit data, or adding a general-purpose computer to an abstract idea, typically does not integrate the exception into a practical application or provide significantly more. Case examples of tool-use: Affinity Labs v. DirecTV (cellular telephone), TLI Communications v. AV Auto (server & telephone unit). Contrasting examples where computer/technology improvement supported eligibility: McRO, Enfish (improvements to computer functioning/technology). See MPEP §§ 2106.04(d)(1) and 2106.05(a) for discussion of technological improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity or generality of the application of the judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how narrowly or broadly the claim applies the judicial exception across fields and whether it confines the exception to a particular, practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims with broad applicability across many fields that recite only the effect or result (or every mode of accomplishing it) likely do not provide meaningful limitations and amount to merely adding 'apply it'. Case examples: Internet Patents v. Active Network (maintaining state generically). By contrast, limitations that confine the exception to a specific practical application (e.g., BASCOM's filtering tool installed at a specific location with user-customizable features) may be meaningful. Historical authorities: O'Reilly v. Morse, The Telephone Cases (monopolizing natural forces/information).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant Extra-Solution Activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether additional elements add only insignificant extra-solution activity—activities incidental to the primary invention (pre-solution or post-solution) that are nominal or tangential and do not amount to an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extra-solution activity examples: pre-solution (gathering data) and post-solution (printing a report). Supreme Court: Parker v. Flook and Mayo — post-solution/conventional activity cannot transform an ineligible principle into a patentable process. Examiners should evaluate claims on their merits and consider other MPEP factors (particular machine/transformation, well-understood routine conventionality, field of use) to assist determination, but should not evaluate well-understood/routine/conventionality in Step 2A Prong Two (that's for Step 2B). If an element adds only insignificant extra-solution activity, explain why it does not meaningfully limit the claim in a rejection (see MPEP § 2106.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the extra-solution limitation is well known
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider if the extra-solution activity is a well-known or conventional technique, which would suggest it is token or nominal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-known activities have been treated as token extra-solution activity (Bilski v. Kappos: known random analysis techniques as inputs; Flook: existing surveying techniques; Intellectual Ventures I v. Erie Indem.: use of a well-known XML tag). Because this overlaps with the well-understood, routine, conventional consideration, do not consider it in Step 2A Prong Two (reserved for Step 2B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the limitation is significant (imposes meaningful limits on the claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess if the limitation imposes meaningful limits such that it is not merely nominal or tangential to the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a limitation meaningfully confines the claim, it may be significant. Examples found insignificant: restricting public access to media (Ultramercial), certain electronic menu features (Ameranth). This significance inquiry is relevant in both Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the limitation amounts to necessary data gathering and outputting
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the limitation is simply necessary data gathering or data output that all uses of the recited judicial exception would require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Necessary data gathering/outputting (e.g., measuring metabolites, presenting offers & gathering statistics, obtaining transaction info to verify credit card transactions) has been treated as insignificant extra-solution activity (Mayo; OIP Technologies; CyberSource v. Retail Decisions). This consideration applies in both Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of Insignificant Extra-Solution Activity (illustrative list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete examples the courts have found to be insignificant extra-solution activity, including mere data gathering, selecting particular data types/sources, and insignificant post-solution applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere data gathering examples: performing clinical tests to obtain equation input (In re Grams); system testing to obtain response data (In re Meyers); presenting offers & gathering response statistics (OIP Technologies); obtaining internet transaction info to verify credit cards (CyberSource); consulting/updating logs (Ultramercial); determining biomarker level in blood (Mayo). Selecting particular data source/type examples: limiting database index to XML tags (Intellectual Ventures I v. Erie Indem.); taking only table-based or drive-through orders (Ameranth); selecting grid information for display (Electric Power Group). Insignificant application examples: cutting hair after determining hairstyle (In re Brown); printing/downloading generated menus (Ameranth). Some cases treat insignificant computer implementation as extra-solution activity (Fort Properties; Bancorp Services), though other cases treat similar limitations as mere instructions to apply an exception—see MPEP § 2106.05(f) for overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of Use and Technological Environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that merely link the judicial exception to a particular field of use or technological environment (i.e., 'apply it' in a technological context) generally do not make the claim patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim cannot be made eligible simply by limiting the formula/exception to a particular technological use or field (Diamond v. Diehr; Parker v. Flook). Field-of-use limitations and token post-solution components do not make an abstract idea patentable. Use Flook and Bilski authorities as classic examples. Evaluate whether the limitation goes beyond mere field-of-use labeling and actually integrates the exception into a practical, technological application.
